text: The sky appears blue because of a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight contains all colors of the visible spectrum, and when it enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with tiny gas molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). These molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of light—like blue and violet—much more strongly than longer wavelengths like red and orange. In fact, blue light is scattered roughly four times more than red light. This scattered blue light bounces around the atmosphere in all directions, so no matter where you look in the sky, blue light reaches your eyes. The sky doesn't appear violet instead, even though violet is scattered even more, because the sun emits less violet light, our eyes are less sensitive to it, and some violet is absorbed in the upper atmosphere. This is also why sunsets look red and orange: when the sun is low, its light travels through more atmosphere, and by the time it reaches you, most of the blue has been scattered away, leaving the warmer colors behind.
